utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now again. Before we resume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it is good that since we are now in open session, that we call the case again, Madam Registrar, although we did that already in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume the testimony of the witness, I would first like to inform the Defence that upon their request to reargue the admission of the report of Mr. Higgs, that five minutes will be granted to that just before the next break. And we still have to decide upon the admission of the documents in respect of witness Arifagic. We already have listed all the documents. Madam Registrar, if you would please closely follow the order. I am trying to keep the order as used yesterday, that would mean that perhaps we do it just by putting together similar documents, that would mean, 3738 A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, are the first documents we will have to decide upon. These are all death certificates. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would you like us to make our objections now or at the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather do it by type of documents. So we have now all the death certificates as I just mentioned. If there are any objections, please submit them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, thank you very much. Mr. Chairman the Defence wishes that document to be rejected and as a consequence we can't accept it for a whole range of reasons. The first being that in most of these documents, that we have classified differently, there are no signatures from no authority whatsoever, either of medical nature or something indicating municipality or an official from the municipality, somebody in charge of the official registers of both the living and the dead. The other thing is that in the case of some documents bearing a signature, I don't believe that that signature had been certified or authenticated by anyone, either from the -- either a Registrar or a doctor authorised to do so. Nothing at all. And something else, very often these documents, or rather the copies of the documents, are of such quality that they are hardly legible and as far as we are concerned, completely useless. And so due to the first two points which are points of substance and the other one which is point of form, we would like for these documents to be rejected. I am just going to consult with my colleague to make sure that I haven't forgotten anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is being pointed out to me that the R and S certificates are not mentioned on your list, so we will come to those later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the death certificates I just mentioned are totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that the certificates as such were totally illegible, I just said that some parts are totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so if you said, "en partie" that means partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next Exhibit would be 3738L from London.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will just consult for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, Mr. President, the same problem here. In other words, we have got a documents which are extremely difficult to read. Sometimes partially illegible and apparently there was -- there is no certified signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... M, which is a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, we have got a list. It doesn't bear any sort of certified signature at all. And due to this reason, we oppose it being tendered. Apart from that, I would just like to draw your attention to something else, a rather important fact. This list includes some purely subjective and biased elements and you will understand in a second. Let me just quote by way of example this one point. In the second line which is just below the name Dobrinja if you can read it, there is a reference of the cause of death and it says "sniper fire, 4294." Sniper bullet means in French a bullet coming from a sniper. But, as a matter of fact, and it will be proven in a minute, no doubt and bullet and to repeat it in English, the bullet, as we call it in English, I can't tell you whether it is a sniper who had fired it or a soldier or whoever else. So this list includes elements of biased judgment which are actually confusing the real state of affairs. Because a bullet as such, can't tell you whether it comes from a sniper or anyone else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 3738N, Nicholas. Next document would be P3738 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now on 38M, we will come back to that later. The Defence tried to do their best in order to understand this. Well, we don't really know, Mr. Chairman, how we can understand. I don't know what you've got here. I have got this copy. This is what I have. And if you manage to translate this, well, I will pay my respects to the translator, because that would mean they have an excellent eyesight. Because these documents are totally illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next document 3738P.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just repeat the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am following the order that was used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will come back -- no, we have got a "P" here in fact. I do apologise. The same as for the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3738R from Rotterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On document "R" Mr. President, we have documents there which bear no official seal and no certified signature, that is to say, no signature by a doctor as such who would be competent to make these statements or a public official. As a consequence, this should be rejected and that applies to document "S" and that will gain us some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: S as in Simon, the next one is 3738T, I think it is, yes, which is a list, last two digit ERN 78 and following.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the speaker, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to check it out. Mr. President, we are raising objections here with reference to the poor quality of the copies we were given. As far as the Defence is concerned, it is therefore impossible for us to check whether these people actually do exist because quite often their addresses or any other type of identification is illegible. For example, on page two or page three, you can't actually read the cause of death. And apart from that, as in the case of the other documents of this sort we consider that the information provided is clearly biased which makes these documents highly suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next document would be 3748.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same comment there on the lack of certification with reference to the document itself in terms of the competence that should be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will see with the Registrar. Is there a translation of this document? No translation tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday I sought permission of the Court to show the document to the witness and question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not tendering?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was not planning to tender it as an exhibit, but -- we could provide the translations during the course of the day, if I am permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then not give a decision yet on this document and we will wait for a translation. And then an indication of whether you want to -- I do understand that you want to tender that document, but then we need a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one would be 3369A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, too, the copies are lacking in clarity, but what we are unable to read are certain words, for example in the second line -- oh, no the fourth line referring to the diagnosis, and the second line, for example, in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I see that the Defence does not object apart from that it notes that there are certain parts that are less legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3747, may I take it that the Defence objects on the basis of illegibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you give them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, we have got certain things which are inadmissible. You were told yesterday at some length that the last -- the latest version of the document 3747.1 was also the same in its form as the one enclosed to the document itself, that is to say, the previous translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... present translation of the translation tendered is the last version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that, Mr. President. What I am trying to say is -- refers to the reading of both documents and this is an important point, in fact. If you take a look at the first document, that is to say the enclosed one, you can see that the fourth name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the first translation we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I am referring to the first translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first translation is not tendered and has been removed and is replaced by the second version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Mr. President. I have grasped that. What I am trying to say is that if we compare these two documents which we have at least received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only issue is whether the translation tendered is an acceptable translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I am going to rephrase this. According to the second translation, well, since the names there are not the same as the names indicated in the first translation, we cannot help wondering about this. Why? Why aren't the names the same? If you wish me to quote an example I will be glad to provide them, if not, it doesn't matter. Not just the names, but I have seen that in the first translation, there are things which could have been translated so there is a clear text somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that a comparison between the first and the second translation is not to be discussed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from that, that document is totally illegible, for the most part. And my third point, this is a document which seems to be an artificial construction. And this is something that we have pointed out to in the past and the Judges have seen it, the dates, for example for as long as -- for as much as we can read them are fabricated. For example, there is a reference to this gentleman called Malicbegovic and we simply don't understand how come all of a sudden, there was a date of the 28th of July 1992 and all of a sudden is inserted into a list which refers to the date of the 1st of June 1993. And from that point of view it appears to us to be particularly striking that apparently this list should be referring to the events of the 1st of June and then all of a sudden, there is this different date which comes up to. So to us, this is an indication that this list had been interfered with and therefore we object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that where I mentioned these documents, that the translations were discussed as well since you made objection against one or more of the translations. I take it that has been dealt with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would you like to respond to the objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, with regard to the objection based on illegibility, if each and every document is taken, most of it is legible. It is that I can say with regard to Exhibit number P3747 is certainly illegible in certain areas of the document. The whole purpose of tendering this as an exhibit was not to go into contents, Mr. President, but to establish that on the 1st of June 1993, so many patients were admitted to the hospital which can be quite clearly seen by the document itself. And in addition to which, the fact that some areas of the document is illegible, does not invalidate those legible areas, the contents that can be deciphered in the legible areas. I say that the objection is without merit on that basis. And the Defence counsel made a sweeping objections to all the documents tendered through this witness, but if each and every document is gone into separately, Mr. President, Your Honours, will see that all are not as illegible as the Defence claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to the absence of signatures of the doctor or a person in certain documents, there are only I think five documents that were pointed out to the witness. The witness clearly stated that she compared these documents with the original documents and that she was satisfied with the authenticity of these copies. And she, the witness has signed these documents certifying the authenticity of these documents. And one must consider these documents in the backdrop of the circumstances in which these documents were created and therefore I move that these documents be admitted in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I would just like to point out in response to my colleague, that the witness in the opinion of the Defence, and we had carefully listened to what has been said she never said that she had compared this document with the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had in mind that we would decide upon the objection and the response, but if there is any specific response to this observation, Ms. Mahindaratne, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I recall the witness repeated that she did compare the documents and that she was satisfied with the authenticity of the documents, that is how I recall. But I do not want to waste the time of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will give a decision on most of the documents right away. As I mentioned before, we are waiting for a translation of P3748. We will not give a decision yet on P3738O, Oslo. Document P3747 will not be admitted as it -- on the basis of its illegibility, but the Prosecution will have an opportunity to file or to submit a -- this document but then better legible and we will then decide on whether that copy could be admitted into evidence. But as it is now, in this present form, it is not admitted. All the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Submission should not be later than the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The submission of a better copy or -- of this document P3747 should not be later than the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the other documents are admitted into evidence. Then is the Prosecution ready to resume the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness is AK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, AK. And we first have to turn into private session, face distortion and we are using the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, may I enquire if before we move on to the discussions in respect to the expert report, if perhaps we could tender P3748.1 with the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps we first given an opportunity, as I indicated, to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to reargue the -- oh, is it about this expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then I would first like to give the opportunity to the Defence to argue on the Higgs report. Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are talking about the expert right? Thank you. First of all, thank you very much for granting us the opportunity to reopen this matter. We would simply like to mention with reference to expert Higgs, we would just like to say that in the case of this expertise, we would have to apply the case history of the case law and very often you've expressed wish to see documents here where there is no contamination or interference. In the course of the cross-examination of expert witness Higgs, Mr. Ierace asked him about the first two events, I believe, and he asked him not to take account of the witness accounts which had been submitted to him at the time. That is to say, witnesses A, B, C on the one hand and B, C, on the other hand I believe. As a consequence what we would like to ask quite simply is for this expertise, every time we see it in writing that there is a reference to these witness accounts with reference to which the Prosecution wanted them to be excluded, for them to be automatically deleted from the text of the expertise. In much the same way as we have done in other similar situations for example, bombs, that is to say bombs dropped from planes, which were excluded from the shelling of Sarajevo. We have done the same thing and Prosecution should present us with a streamlined document in this way. And thank you for granting me the opportunity refer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this in fact not a new argument. This is an argument which Mr. Piletta-Zanin advanced two days ago. He has added nothing. The report, of course, is prepared on the basis of material which may not ultimately reflect the evidence in the trial for a number of reasons. It would be a nonsense to suggest that expert reports which, according to the rules, must be filed in some cases, months before the witness gives evidence can take into account the vagaries of the trial timetable and of course work on the report must begin months before then and, therefore, cannot be comprised entirely, if at all, of the trial evidence. Secondly, Mr. President, this is offered as a reason to not tender the report. The report expresses itself to be based on certain material. In relation to the first shelling incident it is now apparent that the Prosecution will not be calling two of its witnesses which were relied upon in the form of witness statements. I have clearly drawn from the expert witness his opinion in the absence of those two witness statements. Therefore the Trial Chamber is now aware of what his relevant evidence is and is still assisted by his original report in relation to the first schedule where that is still relevant. In relation to the second shelling incident, just a matter of a few minutes ago, certain evidence which was relevant came before the Trial Chamber, I will say no more, and we still await a decision from the Trial Chamber in relation to the second questionable material. Therefore, it may well be that by the time the Prosecution closes its case references A, B, and C, are admitted and therefore that part of the report stands complete. If it transpires that one of those three sources is not, then the Trial Chamber is properly equipped to make the necessary adjustment to the conclusions of the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you one thing: In respect of shelling incident one, do you say that the oral testimony more or less replaces what is in the report or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are some aspects of the written report which are still relevant. There's a simple example, the first sentence. And it is a very simple matter for the Defence, the Trial Chamber to deduce what sentences are still are relevant and what are not, on the basis that certain sentences clearly do not depend on references B and C. It is not a complex exercise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To give a second example, the second sentence also stands unaffected and so on. And in any event, in a summary form, the witness gave his opinion based just on the forensic report. His evidence was clearly to the effect that he understood he was limited to the examination by Mr. Houdet, and his own examination of what remained of the craters when he went to Sarajevo. So there is no problem in a common sense way in deducing what his opinion, putting to one side sources B and C was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your position. As you will understand, we will not immediately give a decision on that and look to the matter in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst I am here, might I briefly raise a timetable issue. The next witness will be Mr. Cekic, pursuant -- who will give his evidence pursuant to the 92 bis decision. In other words, he will be made available for cross-examination by the stipulated period of time followed by the last witnesses in the Prosecution case, the sniping experts, Jonathan Hinchliffe. There are some other matters which we need to attend to before the Prosecution closes its case. Two matters that immediately come to mind are firstly the tender from the bar table by the Prosecution of I think it is around 17 documents and one videotape. I don't know whether the Defence proposes to object to any of that material. If so, we will need to allocate some time for legal argument. And secondly, depending upon the decision of the Trial Chamber in respect of the statement of Zoran Lesic there are some annexures to be provided consequent to that statement. I think that's the 92 bis statement. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Yes. Of course, we will have to find time for that. These are issues still outstanding. We will find the proper time for it. It would not be now. I think we would rather now proceed to give you the opportunity to -- at least to give the Defence the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President could I respectfully suggest and I appreciate the time the Trial Chamber has made available today, that if by the end of the day we clearly have a problem for tomorrow, then perhaps we could sit a little early tomorrow morning, perhaps 8.30. Just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but sitting earlier would engage a lot of practical things such as transportation of the accused, availability of interpreters, et cetera, et cetera. I don't know whether this could be done but at least your suggestion is clear and we will see whether the Chamber is willing to follow the suggestion and whether the Chamber is able to follow your suggestion. Then, Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Cekic into the courtroom. Time set for cross-examination was not more than one hour and a half in our 92 bis decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Although the 92 bis papers have been filed, there are discreet parcels just relevant to his 92 bis proper. These are those copies of the papers that were filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- that is the statement and the annexes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, this is a complete 92 bis package in one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they have been filed. I have got hopefully the same in front of me. If you could please provide them to the Registrar so that it could assist us. Mr. Cekic, I take it. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Cekic, please be seated. Mr. Cekic the Prosecution has presented to the Chamber a copy of your written statement and some annexes, and the Defence has expressed its wish to cross-examine you on that statement. And the Chamber granted the request of the Defence. So, therefore, you will be cross-examined on this statement by the Defence. But perhaps first we distribute the documents. Ms. Pilipovic, is it you or is it Mr. Piletta-Zanin who will cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will start the cross-examination and with your permission, my colleague might add a couple of questions. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, can you tell us where you live and where you work at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo and I work at the University of Sarajevo at the faculty of political science in Sarajevo. I am a lecturer in two subjects, and I am also the director of the institute for the study of the crimes against humanity and international law and I have been there from the very setting up of that institute in 1992, until today. That means at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Mr. Cekic, since you have told us that you are the director of this institute for the investigation of crimes against humanity and international law which was set up in 1992, can you tell us during what period of time, in what month of the year 1992 it was set up?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The institute was set up on the 4th of September 1992 and on the 23rd of October of that same year at the meeting of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina presided over by the deputy head of government Professor Dr. Zlatko Lagumdzija, I was appointed the director of that institute and a couple of days later, I got a letter of appointment in written form confirming my appointment as the director of that newly founded scientific institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Given that you have told us in October 1992 the deputy prime minister appointed you as director, could you tell us how this institute was formed and on whose initiative it was formed?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: It was formed on the initiative of a suggestion that was made by a certain number of scientific and professional workers at the time in Sarajevo this was above all the case because at the time in Sarajevo which was under siege, the civilian population in particular suffered and it was decided that a scientific institute should be formed, a scientific and research institute, which would be involved in the research, the analysis, the processing of all forms of crime, all forms of crime that had been perpetrated or had been perpetrated at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, would you agree with me that up until the time when the conflict broke out, Sarajevo was a multi-ethnic city? And when I say "multi-ethnic" what I said was a multi-ethnic town, I mean that various peoples lived in that town and peoples whose religion was different?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. I didn't understand your question very well. Are you asking me whether I am aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We can also talk about the ethnic composition of the population in approximate terms et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Was your principle formed on this basis too? We are talking about the multi-ethnic principle.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it really was formed on the basis of that principle. And that this is the case if you so wish, I can mention a few facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, could you tell us on what scientific principle was your institute supposed to work, what you have referred to as scientific truth, in your opinion how did it --

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: As I said, the institute was formed as a scientific institute, which means that it was involved in and is involved in research into crimes and to carry out this research it applies scientific methodology which can be found in sciences. This methodology can be found in sciences because this institute was a place where a wide groups of scientists were based, lawyers, demographers, psychologists, various professionals, this also includes a certain number of doctors, gynecologists given -- taken into account certain crimes that were perpetrated. So it was based on the scientific methodology above all because the institute later on and it still is today, it is a scientific institute which is a member of the university in Sarajevo. So like all other faculties, and a certain number of other institutes, such as the institute for history, for languages, for genetics, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, since you have told us that you are appointed as director of that institute, could you tell us whether you directed that institute, or was a body formed at the level of an institute and if so what was the nature of this body which took decisions and supervised the work of that institute?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: At the time of the institute's establishment and later on, today too, there are management bodies within the institute, leadership bodies, and there are supervisory bodies. If we are talking about management or administrative bodies, it is necessary to bear in mind the following fact: This in fact concerns an administrative committee which was also appointed the first administrative committee was appointed by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 23rd of January 1993. And the chairman of that committee was the well known and well respected sociologist Professor Ivan Cvitkovic. If you want me to tell you his nationality is he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cekic, that is why I asked you that question. If there was an administrative body which administered the institute, do you want to tell us that that administrative body was formed and based on a multi-ethnic principle?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. By all means. In addition to the respected chairman, the members of that administrative committee were the following: His deputy was Professor Atif Purivatra among the members was the well known -- certainly you have certainly heard about this name, his is a well known scientist and a well known politician, Mirko Pejanovic and then Professor Nijaz Durakovic, Professor Ivan Lovrenovic and another two members, Dr. Becir Macic and Dr. Munib Maglajlic so if we are talking about the administrative bodies, it is necessary to say that it administered the scientific institute and its competence was very wide. And the administrative committee replaced and could -- it could replace the director. So the director was held accountable for his work by the administrative body, by the administrative committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic, now that you have given us the names of the people who were members of the administrative committee and institute, I understand that there were Croats and Serbs and Muslims in this body so that Mr. Mirko Pejanovic as you said was a Serb, he was a member of that institute. Mr. Cekic you told us that you could tell us what the ethnic composition of the population of Sarajevo was, we will be referring to the year 1992. So could you tell us what it was like at the beginning of the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: To answer your question, I will make use of approximate information from the last population census which was carried out in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Before you answer my question concerning the national composition, the ethnic composition of the population, according to the census from 1991, I would like you to tell me whether you are aware of the fact that according to the census of 1991, was it necessary for that population census to be verified by certain institutes, be that at a republic or a federal level? Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know the results of that census were subsequently made public and those results were published by the statistics institute of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time, and I am referring to 1991, and at that time Yugoslavia still existed, the relevant federal institute for statistics, did that body verify the census apart from the fact that you said that you knew that it was the republican institute of statistics for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but I don't think that that was done, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. Sir, let me return to my question before we start talking about the census. And this regards the national -- the ethnic composition of the population in Sarajevo in 1991 and at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. According to the results that we have discussed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I shall provide you with approximate information. I can't provide you with exact figures. With regard to the number of inhabitants in Sarajevo, that is an area which made up the town of Sarajevo, 10 municipalities. There were 527.000 and a bit, whether it was a bit more or not, I am not quite sure right now. If we are talking about the ethnic composition of a 250.000 or 259.000 and something and a bit, were Muslims. And in that would be 49.3 or .6 per cent. I really can't tell you the exact number of Serbs. It was a little less and the percentage of Croats was even less. And then there was citizens who had declared themselves to be Yugoslavs and there were also -- there was also a category which included others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, on the basis of your answer, we can conclude that in the area of the town of Sarajevo, the Muslims were in the majority and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic at a certain time in 1992, so we are also talking about the beginning of 1992, did the ethnic composition of the population in Sarajevo change in these 10 municipalities? And when I say, did a change occur, as far as you know, did any parts of the population move from one municipality into other municipalities? Did this factor, moving from one municipality to another, change the ethnic composition of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, if we are going to discuss these facts, yes, I think there were such cases. However, in my opinion, and up to now, no one has carried out a scientific or any other kind of analysis in order to be able to provide a complete answer to this question of yours. But what I can claim, what I can say, what I am aware of is the following: Towards the end of 1991 and especially at the beginning of 1992, a certain number of Serbs from the town of Sarajevo from certain parts, from the Vogosca settlement, were I was -- where I lived in 1991 and until May 1992 a certain number of Serbs left their houses left their flats without this being noticed. And this was particularly evident in the evening hours and at night. We noticed this on the basis of the behaviour of our Serb neighbours with whom we were on very good terms. We lived together with them on very good terms. And this is something that we noticed. But, as I said, no one carried out any kind of research into this matter so that it is not possible to provide a serious answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your institute didn't answer?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No my institute hasn't researched this -- hasn't researched this up until now. That is an important subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that Muslims noticed that the Serbian population was leaving certain parts of the city do you connect these movements, this moving out, would you agree that this is the result of the multiparty elections and the referendum which was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina in March, that is to say in February?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. Because that phenomenon appeared even before the referendum. But you must bear in mind the fact that in November in Bosnia-Herzegovina a plebiscite was held, a plebiscite of the Serbian people which had been organised by the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what happened in the Assembly, if you remember, it is what Mr. Karadzic said in the Assembly, he made those threats so there was tension --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. But was that tension related to the formation of the Muslim and Croat coalition?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't provide you with a full answer to that question. According to the results of my research, that coalition really didn't exist and I say it didn't exist because the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as soon as November 1991, on the 18th of November, 1991, to be precise, formed a collaborationist entity which is called Croatia community of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was formed by the regime in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Cekic, you say that is the result of your research. But let me ask you the following: Were you a member of the Serbian -- of the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: For a certain period of time I was formally a member of that party and I say "formally" and that was at a time when at the town level that party was led by the well known professor Sefer Halilovic. He is now the president of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cekic. When you were asked whether you were a member of the SDA -- well, could you tell us whether you are aware of the fact that at the time the SDA in the 1990s formed the Patriotic League, which was a sort of military structure and functioned within the framework of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: That fact is something I am aware of. But I learned about it a lot later. I say a lot later and in far greater detail, especially in the last few years or to be more precise, this year because at my university a certain number of scientific reports are being defended and they deal with political and military situations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The military and political conditions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And one of those reports was recently published at my university where I work and I was a president of the committee which listened to this work, this master's thesis being defended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, we spoke about the appearance of parties in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990 and 1991. We were referring to national parties. Could you tell us in what sense did the ethnic composition of the population change in 1990 and 1991 in the municipalities of the town of Sarajevo in these 10 municipalities we have mentioned, in your opinion. So my specific question is: In your opinion, was there a division of municipalities that was carried out on the basis of the national, the ethnic composition of the population?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The results of the research carried out on the part of our institute revealed that at the time, no division had been carried out on the basis of the ethnic composition of the population, but that in fact, up until -- but in fact there was a division of individual municipalities and this was because of the pressure exerted by military force and to be more specific, by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic we spoke about changes in the population, in the ethnic composition of the population in the 10 municipalities of the town of Sarajevo and you agreed with me that at a certain period of time in 1991 and 1992, some Serbs, Serbs moved out from one part of the town of Sarajevo. At that time, did any Muslims move into certain parts of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know and I think that this is something that I am really familiar with, nothing like this happened until -- well, could you clarify the question, please. If we are talking about the Vogosca and I know the situation there the best, my very good friends and neighbours who left their houses, no one moved into those areas. No one moved in. No one moved into their houses or flats or to the places where they had lived up until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I left Vogosca on the 5th of May 1992, in exceptionally difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, perhaps we shall return to that question later. You as a scientist, could you tell us, given that you told us that you could tell us what the ethnic composition of the population of the town of Sarajevo was, can you tell us with regard to the municipality of Vogosca, what the ethnic composition of the population was there?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I think that over 50 per cent of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a certain point in time in 1992 and I am referring to March and April, were barricades set up in the area of the municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the area of the municipality of Vogosca and it was particularly noticeable there. And let me tell you, I was a witness of these barricades being erected. I saw them especially the barricades that had been set up at the exit from the municipality of Vogosca, when you leave the town, go down the river of Bosna or towards Zenica or Tuzla, when you go towards crossroads - allow me please to finish this sentence - and from the end of 1991, there were JNA units in that area. And the JNA had really organised those barricades and apart from the fact that I personally saw this, the original documents that can prove this is really correct, very reliable documents from certain units and commands in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, since you have answered my question and told me what -- who, in your opinion, set these barricades up, do you know whether certain paramilitary formations which were in the municipality of Vogosca, do you know whether they were also -- whether they also put up barricades, so such units which consisted of Muslims and was there a division in the municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I am really not aware of the existence of such paramilitary formations, but I do know that the most serious problems emerged in the police station in the area of the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, can you tell us what the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality of Vogosca is right now? You said that at the time in 1992 the Muslims were in the majority. So the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality of Vogosca consisted of Serbs. They were also in the majority there. Can you tell us what the ethnic composition of the population is now?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't give you exact figures, exact information because from 1991 up until today, population census has not been made. But what is correct is the following: Even today in the area of the municipality of Vogosca, the Bosniaks represented a greater percentage than the percentage they represented in the census in 1991. And if you like, I can explain the reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, thank you. But if I tell you that according to the census of 1991, 51 per cent of the population was Muslim and 36 per cent was Serb, in this situation, can you provide us with a percentages and tell us what the relationship was, what the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality of Vogosca is?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Maybe over 80 per cent is Bosniak. So the Bosniaks are in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, may I ask you to make a pause between the question and the answer. If you would look at your screen and you see that at a certain moment the cursor stops moving. You are speaking the same language, therefore, it is a bit too quick for the interpreters. And Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you to do the same. And of course, between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, when we were discussing your institute and the setting up of your institute which, as you say, was set up in order to find out the scientific truth and an objective unbiased truth and in order to research crimes against humanity and international law, well, can you tell us with reference to the area of the city of Sarajevo, and I am referring to the period of time 1992, 1993, and 1994, so far what have you established when it comes to these crimes in case there were any?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Within the institute we are currently involved in a number of scientific research projects. Amongst other projects is one entitled "the suffering of Sarajevo in the course of aggression against the Republic of Bosnia in 1992 and 1995."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, I am simply going to tell you that the term "aggression" is a word which is not normally used before the Court and this Chamber, considering that we do know who is -- who has the ability to --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour. I should have asked you to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I think we are in a different situation here. Because the witness tells us the name and the subject of his research. And of course you could put whatever questions about the words used, but that is different from a general reference to an armed conflict. So, therefore, here, I would not direct the witness to use more neutral terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, considering that you have told us that at a certain point your institute, you said, established that there was an aggression. Well, can you tell us, on the basis of what facts did you arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: We arrived at that conclusion on the basis of various sources of information, information of various origin and different nature. First and foremost on the basis of the original materials, documents, papers, referring to the command of the second military area in Sarajevo, and then on the basis of -- or the second military district. And on the basis of the documents referring to the Serb democratic party of Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, our institute is in the position of all the original documents referring to that party ever since it was set up until the 28th of March. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, I am just going to ask you one question. Do you know what body is -- has the capacity to determine the use of the term "aggression"?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: In replying to this question allow me to remind you that this is a scientific institute. We are talking about scientists here, and scientists and research scientists have never sought or and they are never going to seek any opinions from any other bodies or organisations. What you probably have in mind is this court. But I would also like to remind you, if I may --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, I simply asked you to answer my question as to whether you were aware of what body or institution would have the capacity to do that. If you don't wish to answer me or if you don't know the answer, just simply say no. As to your own personal opinions --

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see it is not a matter of my own personal opinion. It is a matter of quite a few research scientists who both in Bosnia itself and in the world has reached its conclusion. And let me remind you of the general resolution of the UN, dated the 18th of December 1992, whereby in several instances the term used is "aggression" and not only that but even the term genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to intervene. If we are talking about the authority who could determine what is aggression and what is not aggression, I would like not to have a debate between the witness and between counsel. But may I perhaps give you some guidance, Ms. Pilipovic. In terms of criminal law, international criminal law, and the establishment on whether a person is responsible for certain acts, it certainly is a court who establishes that. On the other hand, in scientific research, usually terms are defined by the scientists and they can make research. And, of course, there are -- its possible that there is criticism on their definition of certain words. But let's not engage in a debate between the witness and counsel. I am not saying that you are not allowed to ask questions on the subject, but this is not a place where debate where examination of a witness should occur. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, your institute at a certain point in time drew up a questionnaire. Do you have a copy of that questionnaire next to you? First of all, is it correct that you had such a questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: It is correct. I don't have a copy of that questionnaire here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness does have this questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is me you mean? I don't have it. I don't have it. Oh, you mean this one. Okay, I do apologise. Could you just refer me to the page you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is page 15. The Prosecution document is 02156166.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who participated in the drawing up of the questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we are under time pressure. I can see you are writing things down. But could you tell me who participated in drawing up this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: It was the research team, the scientific research team and the members of the team were the following -- would you like me to give you the names? But it was a scientific research team of the institute within the team we had a number of people who were experts in methodology, sociology, law, history, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us with reference to this questionnaire which had to be filled out what facts had to be entered -- just a moment -- with reference to the date of death?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The integral part of this questionnaire were the instructions for use and so there, there was an explanation as to the way in which it had to be filled out and that went for all questions, including the ones you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the makeup of the people that had to process this?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The makeup of the team was a multi-ethnic one. In order to prove that that indeed was the case, I can mention a couple of facts for the sake of example. When we talk about the municipality Marin Dvor, the coordinators who worked on this survey and we had four coordinators there, well, all of them were either Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you distributed 120.000 questionnaires. Can you tell us how many people you had to employ in order to process all of that?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: In order to carry out such a complex and large-scale survey, the institute employed approximately 2000 operators, 2000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they go on a special course?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: All of them had previously received training, that is to say, they attended seminars that we organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who funded the project?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: You will be surprised not just you yourself, but probably everybody else present, when I tell you that for such a massive and large-scale survey, nobody provided any funding at all and we did not actually spend any money on this. If you allow me, I could perhaps Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. elaborate this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Cekic. My next question would be the following: Did the operators fill out the forms, the questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The questionnaire for the most part would have been filled out by the operators themselves and it can be seen on the basis of these instructions for use. But we did have certain instances whereby it was the people's survey themselves who filled out the forms and there were reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your work and in the course of the work of the operators did you have any instances whereby the operators would leave the questionnaires in people's mailboxes in case there was nobody home when they witnessed their home? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: It did in fact happen in a couple of cases. But I did say that the questionnaires for the most part would have been filled out by the operator themselves and also in those cases in which it was the head of the family who was filling out the form, the questionnaire, at the end there was the operator's signature as well. So in case you wish to analyse these questionnaires, you can tell exactly who and in what way was involved in the filling out of these forms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, out of this overall number of 120.000 questionnaires that you have managed to distribute, how many did you get back and process at the institute out of this total?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The institute received approximately 80.000 questionnaires. But let me just clarify this is bit. All 120.000 were not actually distributed to the population. They were simply printed. I mean, the printing press actually gave us as many as 120.000 because we calculated that it would be the approximate number that we might need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many questionnaires you did distribute?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: We distributed out of this overall number of 120.000, we managed to distribute slightly more than 100.000, perhaps 105.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that 80.000 came back?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Just to avoid any misunderstandings, 80.000 questionnaires which were filled out were sent back, but we were sent back the forms which had not been filled out. In some cases, questionnaires which were filled out incorrectly, there were people -- things crossed out, and therefore they were not considered valid and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically you are telling us that at your institute you don't process the questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I am just going to speak a bit more slowly because of the interpretation. At the institute, unfortunately, and I would like to stress, unfortunately, to my great regret, we never processed or analysed this data, first of all, due to the lack of funding because, unfortunately, once again, in politics this sort of scientific research is not taken account of to a sufficient extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us on the basis of what data since you were not involved in the processing of the data have you reached the conclusion that some of them were filled out incorrectly, that were blank spaces and things were being crossed out and that 80.000 were sent back to you?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: After the time when certain local communities did process these questionnaires, we got a written reports from the local communities and those reports referred to the following data: First of all, they mentioned we got that many questionnaires from the institute, for example, for the municipality of Vogosca, I can tell you, roughly, 1.700 questionnaires. Then they went on to say as many as 609 were actually filled out or 690. Such-and-such a number were not filled out. Such-and-such a number were filled in incorrectly, and in certain reports, there was also the reference to the fact that a certain number of questionnaires was considered null and void, and such forms were sent back to us. So and their serial numbers were indicated as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I intervene. I get the feeling, but I don't know whether this is true or not, that processing, as it reads in the transcript in English, is used in different ways by you questioning and by the witness answering the questions. It is my understanding that processing could mean the processing of the data in the form, well, let's say, in computers, without analysing them; and another understanding of the word processing might be to analyse them and to draw conclusions out of that. I get the feeling, but just tell me if I am wrong, that when the witness said that they unfortunately have not been in a position to process the data, that he mentioned analysing and drawing conclusions, while the other parties selecting those forms filled in well, perhaps putting the data into computers, but not yet analysing, just processing in a rather technical way and not in an analytical way, it seems that there might be some confusion about what in English is said to be processing. May I ask the attention both of the witness and of you, Ms. Pilipovic, for my feelings. And if I am wrong, please indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I suppose your comment is to the point, but let me put this question again to Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, did you at any point in time carry out the analysis of the questionnaires that you circulated in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: If you mean the analysis that the Presiding Judge was referring to, that is to say, an analytical analysis this is something which has never been done at the institute so far. Never, I said, unfortunately never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cekic, you quoted an example of the municipality of Vogosca. When you mentioned Vogosca, well, could you specify what you meant by the area or the territory of the municipality of Vogosca at the time?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Vogosca, according to the census of 1991, had between seven and eight local communities. I am not quite certain. And our research was carried out or to put it in another way, referred only to the area of two such local communities, called Kobilja Glava and Hotonj, two local communities, that is, that were under siege or rather under the control of the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the rest of the municipality were occupied. And this is the terminology we use in our research and obviously we could not carry out any research in that part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your research referred to two local communities only?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: If we are referring to the territory of the municipality of Vogosca, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, could I ask you a couple of questions about the work of your institute, since you did say that it was multi-ethnic and multinational institute which is based on scientific truth. In the course of your work at the institute, have you established whether in the part of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the BH army there were any crimes committed against the other ethnic groups? What I mean, specifically, is the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: The goal of this research, both in this case and with reference to the overall project, the project as a whole, well, the goal was to establish the number of Serb victims, either the people being killed or the ones who disappeared since we have a whole range of different terms, killed, missing, or whatever. So that was our goal in the past and it is still our goal at the moment. This is an ongoing effort and we are still doing research with reference to a whole range of municipalities in Sarajevo. So our aim is to establish the names and surnames of every individual victim. From our point of view, from a purely scientific point of view, every single victim has a name and a surname and that is the most significant point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your research at the institute, did you find any data, according to which in 1992, 1993, 1994, and the part of Sarajevo which we said was under the control of the BH army, there were any concentration camps or an prisons?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: According to the results of our research so far, I can tell you for certain that in that area, in that part of Sarajevo, there had been no concentration camps. There had been prisons since we have a legal prison institutions which were in existence before the hostilities in much the same way as they tend to exist in every normal country. When you talk about concentration camps, this is something that we haven't heard of so far. But once the project is completed I am sure we will get the final answers to your question considering the fact that in the media some ideas of this sort are being banded about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many Serbs there are in Sarajevo at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I can't really tell you how many there are at this present moment. But what I can tell you for certain is the number of Serbs in Sarajevo, and when I say in "Sarajevo" what I have in mind is all the municipalities, that is to say, 10 municipalities of the city of Sarajevo and I can tell you that the number of Serbs is on the increase on a daily basis and this is something which should be welcomed and this is a price worthy fact and we are doing all we can in Sarajevo, that is to say, the current authorities in Sarajevo are doing their best in order to encourage the Serbs who might have left the city for whatever reason to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just going to ask one more questions and my colleague will have a couple of questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, let's have a break. If this would be your final question we will --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a single question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cekic, how much does your institute do in order to research the crimes against Serbs in Kazani?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Madam, I can tell you, and this is a public and responsible statement that our institute will find an answer to this question and, yes, we are involved in research in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes and resume at 10 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume the examination of the witness, I would like to inform the parties, first about a decision, an oral decision, a written decision will follow, that is that the 92 bis statement of Mr. Lesic will not be admitted in evidence. And as far as tomorrow concerns, until now, there are no practical objections against starting at 8.30. So the Chamber asks the parties to prepare for a start of 8.30 tomorrow morning. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes Mr. President. We are going to profit in order to raise a question at 8.30, in case your Trial Chamber can decide in the course of the day, that it might be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to put a question at 8.30 tomorrow morning? I didn't follow it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. President, I just said it could be 8.32 or 33, but I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that when we commence tomorrow, we would like to talk about a question that will be at 8.30, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If no other matters that keep the Chamber away from this courtroom, always in respect of the case itself, sometimes we need the few time we have to discuss and sometimes that even continues until the very last minute. If it would then be 8.32, you would have to wait until 8.32. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will try to be brief. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. I would like to question you about your questionnaire, about the form of your questionnaire. And when I say, "your questionnaire" we are referring to the questionnaire that we have called the questionnaire for the census of 1994. 94. Do you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: As far as I have understood you, are you referring to the document on the census of the population in 1994? I don't have this document here. Or could you be a little clearer, please. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just said the census relating to 1994. 94.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of family households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to turn to it?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Allow me to find the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness my first question: Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No I don't speak English. I can understand quite a lot, but I don't speak the language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Who translated the English commentary, could you please tell us that?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Was your department involved in this? Did your department translate this or were other persons charged with this task?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No one from the institute's team translated this questionnaire into English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us what the point of the report is, which is in relation with the members -- with family members who were wounded or, what is worse, were on the site where this happened? Could you please tell me what these two points are.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me find this. That is question number six, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said five and six, relating to the wounded and people who are deceased. Thank you, witness. In the 4th column or rather the 5th column relating to these two points there is the word "mesto [phoen]" which means place, or if you write it differently, "measto [phoen]" this is for the wounded and for those who were killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of scientific research, this is of exceptional importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. From the point of view of the Defence too, you can well imagine that. Is it true to say that we can say -- that we can read on each occasion, "the site of the incident" is that correct or not? The place of the incident.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say the place of the incident or event, but it quite clearly says the place where a certain person was killed or rather the place where a certain person in the second case, was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This column was, for the most part, filled in, not by the heads of households, but on each occasion by one of the 2000 assistants responsible for carrying out this investigation. Is that correct? Responsible for carrying out this questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I have already answered this question. A similar question was put to me by your colleague before you and on the whole this part was also filled in by the investigators in the field, people who lived in the area of a certain local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you answer yes or no, we would appreciate that, were any specific instructions given to these investigators; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No specific or special instructions were given to them, apart from the instructions which formed an integral part of this questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, how is it that, as a general rule, there is no more precise indication, for example with regard to municipalities or streets or the street number or the place where such-and-such an incident occurred? First of all, have you understood my question correctly?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Sir this part was sufficient, it was sufficiently clear for someone to be able to mention precisely where a certain person was killed or was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, don't you think that this -- that this would have been a lot clearer if one had indicated the street and perhaps the number and maybe even the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And that should have been done in this situation. It would be necessary to see one or more questionnaires that had been filled in and try and check what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, where are all the 105.000 copies, approximately, of this form that were returned to you? Where is their physical location?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean, "where are they"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to listen to the Serbian translation. Where are they located? Where are they located?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: All these questionnaires are being stored in the institute, in the premises of our institute in Sarajevo and you too can have access if you want to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Willingly, you know these documents and my question is as follows: Under the part, under the column, "the place of the incident where people were wounded or where they were killed" do you often see the name of a street and a number under this heading? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: No I don't because the institute didn't carry out an analytic -- analytic processing of that information at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, did you take these documents somewhere to hand them over to a representative of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, did we take them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean to say, did you yourself, did your department hand over copies of these forms, copies that had been filled in, to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: At their request, we made these -- this research of ours accessible to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you let them take note of the research, but did you or did you not provide them with the 105.000 documents that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: That number of documents, we never handed over that number -- that quantity of documents to them. But we did provide them with a lesser figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the number of documents that you provided them with?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I can't tell you what the exact figure is because that was a task that was carried out by the secretary of my institute on behalf of the institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you give me an approximate figure, please.

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: I really can't be precise. I think that this concerns questionnaires which refer to the situation in two or three municipalities. But I really can't answer you with precision at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who was responsible for informing the Prosecution about, it appears, only two or three municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
utterances.text: That was the -- it was the secretary in the institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this information only referred to two or three municipalities, that is what you are saying, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SMAIL CEKIC
